author: ovi256
cardQuote: This is the kind of startup that withers after the next platform update. Do they have some secret sauce that enables them to offer way more value than a vanilla IM app?
quote: This is the perfect example for "picking pennies in front of a charging steamroller". IM is already chosen as infrastructure by platform makers (Apple, Facebook), given that they've integrated in into their offerings. This is the kind of startup that withers after the next platform update. Do they have some secret sauce that enables them to offer way more value than a vanilla IM app ? That's their only escape route.
storyTitle: WhatsApp bucks convention, quietly builds a messaging titan
outcome: Acquired by Facebook for $19B in 2014; 2B+ users.
outcomeDetail: WhatsApp became the default messaging app in much of the world, was bought by Facebook for $19 billion in 2014, and passed 2 billion users. Its phone-number graph and cross-platform simplicity beat the free alternatives.
note: ovi256 correctly saw that platform messaging was a steamroller, then bet on the steamroller. WhatsApp's phone-number graph and cross-platform simplicity made it the exception.

author: allertonm
cardQuote: to mandate this style is basically asking developers to manually rewrite all of their logic into continuation passing style. It's a bit, well... naive is the kindest word that comes to mind.
quote: (Comment repeated from proggit, where this was also posted.) Don't get me wrong here, I love coding in Javascript and have often entertained the idea that server-side Javascript would be fun. I also totally buy the need to get away from thread-per-request for many web serving scenarios, Comet being a perfect example. However when I see someone going so far with this as to say "all APIs must be non-blocking" I have to wonder if they would be better served by using a language where threads were less expensive. I know closures make this kind of thing a lot less of a pain than back in the day when we were programming against OSs with no threads and async APIs were often a necessity, but to mandate this style is basically asking developers to manually rewrite all of their logic into continuation passing style. It's a bit, well... naive is the kindest word that comes to mind. BTW, I don't think it's a coincidence that all of these event-driven web frameworks are for interpreted languages with crappy thread support.
outcome: One of the most-used runtimes; npm became the largest package ecosystem.
outcomeDetail: Node.js made JavaScript a first-class server language and now underpins a huge share of web tooling. The npm registry it spawned grew to more than a million packages and tens of billions of monthly downloads.
note: allertonm was right that callback style is viral and painful. He was wrong that it would keep Node from becoming the default server-side JavaScript runtime.

author: vicaya
cardQuote: Interesting so far besides some syntax ugliness and lack of macros, but not yet good enough for many system programming projects, especially given the state of the garbage collector.
quote: The home page touts "safety" as a feature the language but all it takes to crash the program is concurrent access to the builtin map: "uncontrolled map access can crash the program", according the faq. Interesting so far besides some syntax ugliness and lack of macros, but not yet good enough for many system programming projects, especially given the state of the garbage collector. GC is the hardest thing to implement large-scale, concurrent, memory intensive applications (e.g, database servers). Java spent 18 years to perfect its GC to be the current state of the art, which still sucks for these applications. I hope they can come up with a concurrent garbage collector that can work on > 16 GBs of RAM with sub ms max latency :)
outcome: Docker and Kubernetes are written in Go; Go 1.0 shipped in 2012.
outcomeDetail: Go launched in November 2009 and reached 1.0 in March 2012. Its standard library, fast builds and goroutines made it the language of cloud infrastructure; Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform and Prometheus are all written in Go.
note: The map crash and GC concerns were real early limitations. Go fixed enough of them to become the language of cloud infrastructure.

author: mikece
cardQuote: After looking over the website briefly I'm still trying to figure out if this is a joke or not.
quote: My first thought is this was a rehast of the js2js joke: https://eleks.github.io/js2js/ After looking over the website briefly I'm still trying to figure out if this is a joke or not. It's only after reading more that it's clear this is a transpiler. Not the clearest of communication.
storyTitle: Swc – Fast JavaScript to JavaScript compiler
outcome: Became Next.js's default compiler and a core Rust toolchain.
outcomeDetail: Next.js 12 replaced Babel with SWC, reporting roughly 3x faster Fast Refresh and 5x faster builds. SWC is also used by Deno, Parcel, and Rspack, and it now sees tens of millions of weekly npm downloads.
note: mikece's confusion was about presentation, not the compiler. SWC became the engine under Next.js and a standard part of the Rust front-end stack.

author: ddevault
cardQuote: The compiler and stdlib is immature. This seems like the first programming language the guy has written. You should have a few failures to learn from before you make a Serious Programming Language imo.
quote: I spent some time with Zig a while ago. Here are my conclusions: - The string handling is braindead - The compiler and stdlib is immature. This seems like the first programming language the guy has written. You should have a few failures to learn from before you make a Serious Programming Language imo. - Code run at compile time is a neat idea but has a weird syntax and really really complicates the internals of the compiler and related tooling. Unfortunately this is no C replacement IMO.
storyTitle: Zig Programming Language 0.1.1: First beta release
outcome: Bun, TigerBeetle and Ghostty are written in Zig; Zig 0.14 shipped in 2025.
outcomeDetail: Zig's first beta landed in 2017 and the language attracted serious infrastructure projects. Bun's JavaScript runtime, TigerBeetle's database and Ghostty's terminal are all written in Zig, and the Zig Software Foundation funds full-time work.
note: ddevault's review was specific and brutal. Zig's compiler and stdlib did mature, and Bun made it a production language.

author: oldguysrule
cardQuote: I suspect it will die in a couple years, like the misguided effort to get people to adopt the Java bridge or WebScript before that.
quote: Objective C isn’t going anywhere. Swift is shit. I suspect it will die in a couple years, like the misguided effort to get people to adopt the Java bridge or WebScript before that.
outcome: Swift was open-sourced in 2015 and became the default language for iOS and macOS; Swift 6 shipped in 2024.
outcomeDetail: Apple announced Swift at WWDC 2014 and open-sourced it the next year. It became the default language for iOS and macOS, expanded to server-side work through Vapor, and reached Swift 6 in 2024.
note: oldguysrule was not alone in thinking Swift was another Apple bridge language. It became the default way to build iOS and macOS apps.

author: sensanaty
cardQuote: In any moderately sized codebase it's basically useless indeed. Pretty much all the praise and hype I ever see is from people making todo-list-tier applications and shouting with excitement how this is going to replace all of humanity.
quote: In any moderately sized codebase it's basically useless indeed. Pretty much all the praise and hype I ever see is from people making todo-list-tier applications and shouting with excitement how this is going to replace all of humanity. Hell, I still have to remind it (Cursor) to not give me fucking React a few messages after I've already told it to not give me React (it's a Vue application with not a single line of React in it). Genuinely maddening, but the infinite wisdom of the higher ups forces me into wasting my time with this crap
outcomeDetail: Claude Code became one of the fastest-adopted developer tools in Anthropic's history, turning the terminal into an agent workspace and pushing competitors toward CLI agents.
note: sensanaty's anger was about codebase scale, not the demo. Claude Code became Anthropic's fastest-growing developer product and pushed the whole industry toward terminal agents.

author: toomuchtodo
cardQuote: My assumption (based on the last few tech IPOs) is that late stage investors are putting lipstick on a pig and trying to get out the door before the music stops.
quote: My assumption (based on the last few tech IPOs) is that late stage investors are putting lipstick on a pig and trying to get out the door before the music stops. https://mattermark.com/2015s-tech-ipos-performing-even-worse... And Steve Blank: > Steve Blank on the Tech Bubble: 'VCs Won't Admit They're in a Ponzi Scheme' http://www.inc.com/zoe-henry/steve-blank-tech-bubble-burst-p...
outcome: IPO'd in 2016; $4.46B revenue and 325K customer accounts in 2024.
outcomeDetail: Twilio went public in June 2016 and grew into a communications platform with $4.46 billion in 2024 revenue and more than 325,000 active customer accounts. Pricing pressure was real, but Twilio's developer ecosystem and product breadth kept it at the center of the market.
note: The IPO pop and subsequent growth made the pig-lipstick line look silly. The pricing pressure he sensed was real, though: Twilio's gross margins and stock never escaped it.

author: weego
cardQuote: I don't know what this could ever do that isn't easily reproducible with a tiny fraction of that investment.
quote: I don't know what this could ever do that isn't easily reproducible with a tiny fraction of that investment. Fragmentation of communities is an absolute given in software. Added to the fact that of they get too dominant they'll get leveraged out of the supply chain and I'm not sure what the value proposition is here. I mean obviously I'll be wrong but it's hard to not be skeptical
storyTitle: Hugging Face raises $235M from investors including Salesforce and Nvidia
outcome: Nvidia agreed to buy Hugging Face for $12.93B in 2026.
outcomeDetail: Hugging Face became the default home for open-weight models, datasets, and demos. In September 2026, Nvidia agreed to acquire it for $12.93 billion, citing its role in the open AI ecosystem.
note: weego was right that model hosting is reproducible. He underestimated the network effect of being the default place where open models, datasets, and demos live.

author: eddsh1994
cardQuote: I just tried Perplexity and it's not very good. For example, ask it a question about a board game you play or how to write a modal in React that gives you a users input and its responses are inaccurate at best.
quote: I just tried Perplexity and it's not very good. For example, ask it a question about a board game you play or how to write a modal in React that gives you a users input and its responses are inaccurate at best. For Ukraines latest news it just told me to check out Al Jazeera.
outcome: Perplexity reached a $20B valuation and 45M monthly users.
outcomeDetail: Perplexity turned the prompt-plus-search pattern into a consumer answer engine with citations, then added Deep Research and a browser. By late 2025 it had about 45 million monthly users, 780 million monthly queries, and a $20 billion valuation.
note: The product really was weak on niche factual questions in early 2023. Perplexity fixed enough of that to become a consumer answer engine at a $20B valuation.

author: staunch
cardQuote: I'm a potential customer who just doesn't see the value proposition. I'm sure they can build a business as a Sendgrid competitor, but I don't see anything as disruptive as Twilio here.
quote: SES is extremely easy, and I seriously doubt any claims that they're more reliable/faster than what Amazon is offering. What kind of intelligent processing are they offering? In the use case of turning a reply into a comment the hard work is not receiving and parsing the email, it's authenticating the user/adding the comment to the database. I'm a potential customer who just doesn't see the value proposition. I'm sure they can build a business as a Sendgrid competitor, but I don't see anything as disruptive as Twilio here.
storyTitle: Mailgun (YC W11) Raises $1.1 Million For Its "Twilio For Email"
outcome: Acquired by Rackspace, then part of Sinch's $1.9B Pathwire deal.
outcomeDetail: Mailgun was acquired by Rackspace in 2012 and later became part of Pathwire, which Sinch bought for about $1.9 billion in 2021. It remained a major transactional email API, delivering hundreds of billions of emails a year.
note: staunch was right that email APIs were not as hard as telephony. Mailgun still became a core piece of transactional email infrastructure and a $1.9B acquisition.

author: cbenz
cardQuote: Indeed I can't see the point of shipping the "AI first" feature as a whole editor. It seems to me that it should be a feature of any editor, or else I'd like to be convinced by arguments less marketing oriented than those I see on the home page.
quote: Indeed I can't see the point of shipping the "AI first" feature as a whole editor. It seems to me that it should be a feature of any editor, or else I'd like to be convinced by arguments less marketing oriented than those I see on the home page.
outcomeDetail: Cursor turned the VS Code fork into an AI-native editor and became one of the fastest-growing software companies ever. It was valued at $29 billion in 2025.
note: cbenz thought AI belonged inside existing editors, not in a new one. Cursor's fork of VS Code became one of the fastest-growing software products ever.

author: d0m
cardQuote: I really don't see how it's big or why YC invested in it. Sure, it's useful. Sure, it's cool. But I'm afraid that it doesn't solve a big enough problem.
quote: Mind to share your mind about how "they are onto something big"? Unless there is a hidden feature somewhere, I really don't see how it's big or why YC invested in it. Sure, it's useful. Sure, it's cool. But I'm afraid that it doesn't solve a big enough problem. Obviously, I'm saying that based on my own experience and knowledge: - As a developer, integrating the various analytic libraries is trivial. Installing it? (npm install mixpanel) is mostly trivial too. Yes, it'll take a couple hours, but it will still take several hours to set up Segment too. (One might argue that's not true, but that's wrong. Even if you include the Segment.io code, you still need to provide a bunch of options and understand very well all the other analytic libraries.) - As a manager, I don't want yet another 30$ or 150$ / month when I'm already paying that for the other analytic services. Also, I know for a fact that I can easily find a dev to set up all the analytics for less than 200$. - As an investor, I ask myself: What's their unfair advantage? It seems like everyone could do such a service and even provide an open-source version of it. So, yeah, I'm a bit lost. I feel it's a big like Grove.io. I really liked the idea and found it very useful. But I didn't see how it'd work as a business. But then, there are hundreds of huge companies that I don't even get their business model. (Twitter?) So, please don't take this comment as a rent, but more as an eye-opener for me to learn about where I'm thinking wrong : )
storyTitle: Segment.io (YC S11) Lets Developers Integrate Multiple Analytics Services
outcomeDetail: Segment became the customer-data pipe behind hundreds of analytics tools—the opposite of a challenge. Twilio bought it for $3.2B in 2020.
note: d0m's math treated analytics integration as a one-off dev task. Segment turned it into infrastructure, then a $3.2B acquisition.

author: jaredcwhite
cardQuote: Can I install this locally? Will it work without an internet connection? Is it fully open source? From what I can tell, the answer to all three questions is no. Is it yet another example of vendor lock-in? Yes.
quote: Can I install this locally? Will it work without an internet connection? Is it fully open source? From what I can tell, the answer to all three questions is no. Is it yet another example of vendor lock-in? Yes.
outcome: Expanded to Postgres and brought the Drizzle team aboard.
outcomeDetail: PlanetScale launched managed Postgres in 2025 and kept investing in its Vitess-based MySQL product. In 2026 the Drizzle ORM team joined the company, and PlanetScale shipped a $5 database tier.
note: The lock-in critique was fair: PlanetScale is a managed service. The company kept expanding rather than collapsing, adding Postgres and acquiring the Drizzle team.

author: romanovcode
cardQuote: I used it in prod for couple of months, then all of a sudden it stopped working, could not figure out how to fix it since there is not so much information on the web. Removed and installed latest nginx. In my opinion it's not prod-ready.
quote: I used it in prod for couple of months, then all of a sudden it stopped working, could not figure out how to fix it since there is not so much information on the web. Removed and installed latest nginx. In my opinion it's not prod-ready.
storyTitle: Caddy – HTTP/2 Web Server with Automatic HTTPS
outcome: Became a widely used web server with 79k+ GitHub stars and automatic HTTPS as its signature feature.
outcomeDetail: Caddy 2 shipped in 2020 with a cleaner architecture and is now a common default in self-hosted and container stacks. W3Techs counted Caddy on 0.2% of scanned sites by 2026—hundreds of thousands of sites—and the project passed 79,000 GitHub stars.
note: romanovcode's production experience was real, and Caddy 0.x was rough. Caddy 2 fixed the architecture and became a common default in self-hosted stacks.

author: micahbule
cardQuote: Personally, I'd still pick NextJS any time for any enterprise-level projects. Remix would be a fun little new framework to toy with for personal projects.
quote: While it is easy to use cache headers with NextJS -- as you said -- you have to know what you're doing. It still boils down to use case, implementation, and quite possibly preference. Personally, I'd still pick NextJS any time for any enterprise-level projects. Remix would be a fun little new framework to toy with for personal projects.
storyTitle: Remix – A framework focused on web fundamentals and modern UX
outcome: Shopify acquired Remix in 2022; Remix merged with React Router in 2024.
outcomeDetail: Remix open-sourced in November 2021 and was acquired by Shopify less than a year later. Its loader and action model influenced React Router v7, which absorbed Remix in 2024.
note: micahbule filed Remix under 'fun little framework for personal projects'. Shopify bought it within a year, and its data-loading model was absorbed into React Router.

author: fapjacks
cardQuote: It's not a question of whether or not ETH (and now the "DAO") is a scam. It is probably a scam. The question is whether or not ETH/DAO can become entrenched as <something> before it dies.
quote: It's not a question of whether or not ETH (and now the "DAO") is a scam. It is probably a scam. The question is whether or not ETH/DAO can become entrenched as <something> before it dies. As someone that got in this game early and has watched altcoins for years, that is pretty much the whole history of ETH, folks. Just do some research.
storyTitle: Autonomous corporation “The DAO” has become the biggest crowdfunded project
outcome: Hacked in June 2016 for ~$50M; Ethereum hard-forked to reverse it.
outcomeDetail: An attacker drained roughly 3.6 million ETH, worth about $50 million at the time, from The DAO in June 2016 by exploiting a reentrancy bug. The Ethereum community responded with a contentious hard fork that reversed the theft and split the chain into Ethereum and Ethereum Classic.
note: The scam label was too broad, but the death call was right: The DAO was drained within weeks and dissolved. ETH survived the fork.

author: risyachka
cardQuote: But if we are talking Firebase - most users want exactly the opposite - they don't want to host their own servers. And when comparing your cloud to Firebase - you won't be able to compete on price.
quote: My point is that sure, there is a valid use case for your service, for people who are looking for an open-source alternative they can host. But if we are talking Firebase - most users want exactly the opposite - they don't want to host their own servers. And when comparing your cloud to Firebase - you won't be able to compete on price. And probably on features and integrations. They've been building that for many years now. All I am saying is it not comparable to Firebase. But lots of people want their own hosted backend they can extend, or will be glad to pay extra for your cloud and for your unique features.
storyTitle: Supabase (YC S20) – An open source Firebase alternative
outcome: Reached 4M developers and a $5B valuation in 2025.
outcomeDetail: Supabase became a default backend for AI app builders such as Lovable and Bolt, and its Series E valued it at $5 billion. Row-level security and database functions remained controversial, but they did not sink the platform.
note: risyachka was right that most Firebase users don't want to self-host. Supabase won them anyway by offering a managed cloud with Postgres and an open-source escape hatch.
